peer_comps_note: We have replaced the supplied peer note's multiples with live ones, because the supplied note is wrong in a way that would have flattered this name. It states that Booking's 15 times free cash flow is 'roughly in line with or modestly cheap' against Airbnb and Expedia, which 'often trade in a similar-to-higher range'. On today's figures Expedia trades at 6.3 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 8.1 times profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - less than half Booking's 14.2 and 12.5 times. Booking is not cheap against Expedia; it is at a large premium, and a premium it earns, since Expedia produces a 26% return on invested capital against Booking's 71%, carries more debt and is growing more slowly. Airbnb is the multiple that supports the case: 19.6 times free cash flow and 31.6 times profit, and that headline understates the gap because Airbnb charges 12.9% of revenue to stock-based compensation against Booking's 2.1%. Deduct that non-cash pay from both and Airbnb trades near 30 times cash generation while Booking trades near 15 - half the multiple for three times the return on capital and a fraction of the dilution. That is the one genuinely defensible relative-value lever here, and it is what sets the 17-times multiple on the merchant engine in our parts valuation. One important qualification, and it is the reason we do not credit the full gap as company-specific edge: the whole online travel cohort is de-rating together on the same unresolved question - whether assistants route around booking platforms. Booking's discount to its own history is therefore largely shared-sector movement on a single unresolved driver, not an idiosyncratic mispricing of this company alone. Treat the gap to Airbnb as a quality-adjusted relative-value observation, not as isolated alpha in this name.
interrogator_dossier:
# Booking Holdings (BKNG) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
*Six consecutive earnings calls, 2025-04-29 through 2026-08-04, cross-referenced against the reported financials. Price used throughout: $170.32 per share (Nasdaq, in US dollars, live quote as of 2026-09-22). Note the company completed a 25-for-1 stock split on 2026-04-06, so all per-share figures here are on the post-split basis.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story did not change. The numbers underneath it did.**

Across six calls, Glenn Fogel and Ewout Steenbergen told one continuous story with four pillars: the Connected Trip (getting a traveller to book more than one thing — a room plus a flight plus a car — in a single place), the Genius loyalty programme, geographic expansion into the United States and Asia, and artificial intelligence. Not one pillar was introduced and quietly dropped. Not one was renamed. That is rarer than it sounds, and it is a genuine credibility marker.

What *did* change is the emphasis and the arithmetic.

**Early in the window (first half of 2025), the tone was offensive.** The first-quarter 2025 call led with a record — "the first quarter we have ever exceeded 300 million room nights" — and the AI discussion was almost entirely about *opportunity*: smart filters, review summaries, a partner assistant. When an analyst raised agentic AI as a threat, Fogel's answer was expansive and almost gleeful: "Maybe what will happen is we'll end up with a whole bunch of them, which is going to be a lot more supply for new customers to be coming, which will lower the cost for us to acquire them. That could be wonderful for us."

**By the third-quarter 2025 call, the framing shifted from opportunity to positioning.** Asked directly by Trevor Young of Barclays whether competitive intensity would pick up over two to three years, Fogel answered with history rather than numbers — a recitation of TripAdvisor, of Meta, of mobile — closing with "I actually see us in a much better position than we were years ago, decades ago." That is a confident answer. It is not a quantified one.

**By the fourth-quarter 2025 call, a defensive edge appeared for the first time.** Fogel walked through the European regulatory alphabet unprompted — "you got DSA, DMA, DFA, EU, AIA, P2B, DAC7, I can go on and on, and that's just the EU" — to argue that large language models will not come down the funnel to where Booking operates. The argument is a good one. But the fact that it needed making, at length, without being asked in those terms, marks the point where the AI question stopped being a growth story and became a defence.

**By the second-quarter 2026 call (2026-08-04), the company was leading with AI as a strategic priority in its own right** — a full section of prepared remarks about working "closely with leading AI organizations to ensure travellers can engage with our brands wherever their journey begins." The most important disclosure of the entire six-call window sits in the Q&A of that call, from Steenbergen: traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid combined, is "still significantly below 1% of our room nights. And that hasn't moved so much recently."

**A second, quieter arc runs underneath: a war arrived and stayed.** The Middle East conflict began at the end of February 2026. It cost roughly two percentage points of room-night and gross-bookings growth in the first quarter of 2026, "a bit higher" in the second quarter, and is assumed to keep pressuring flight prices and long-haul capacity through the third quarter. Management's full-year guidance now embeds seven of twelve months of that impact.

**A third arc is capital allocation, and it became the loudest voice on the call.** Buybacks moved from a footnote to a headline. In the first quarter of 2026 the company repurchased a record $3.6 billion; in the second quarter, $3.7 billion, with $4.1 billion of total shareholder returns. Fogel put an unusual number on the record: share count down more than 40% since 2014, at an average purchase price of $93 per share.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We exceeded the high end of our guidance across all of our key financial metrics" | Q2 2026 | Revenue $7.35B, adjusted EBITDA ~$2.6B, adjusted earnings per share $2.54. The screener records seven earnings beats in seven quarters. | **Matches.** The beat pattern is real and unbroken. |
| Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded 193 basis points in full-year 2025 | Q4 2025 | Full-year 2025 revenue $26.92B against adjusted EBITDA above $9.9B — a 36.9% margin. Trailing-twelve-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA of 12.5x implies about $10.8B of EBITDA today, so the margin has held while revenue grew. | **Matches.** |
| "Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded nearly 40 basis points" in the quarter | Q2 2026 | Reported operating income $2.50B on $7.35B revenue (34.0%) against $2.25B on $6.80B (33.1%) a year earlier — about 90 basis points on the reported line. | **Matches, conservatively stated.** |
| Room-night growth is healthy | Throughout | 7% (Q1 2025) → 8% → 8% → 9% (Q4 2025) → 6% (Q1 2026) → **5% (Q2 2026)**, with third-quarter guidance of **3% to 5%**. | **Diverges.** This is a clean, monotonic deceleration over five quarters. "Healthy" is doing real work in that sentence. |
| The Connected Trip is the strategic engine | Throughout | Connected-trip transaction growth: 35% (Q1 2025) → "over 30%" → "mid-20%" → "high 20% range" for the full year → "high teens" (Q1 2026) → **"low double-digit"** (Q2 2026). | **Diverges sharply.** The flagship strategic metric has decelerated in every single quarter of the window, from 35% to roughly 11%. Management reframes it each time ("more than twice the rate of Booking.com's total transaction growth") rather than address the trend. |
| Alternative accommodations are a core growth driver | Throughout | Room-night growth 12% (Q1 2025) → 10% (Q2 2025) → 8% supply growth (Q4 2025) → **4% (Q2 2026)**, now growing *slower* than the company overall. | **Diverges.** Asked about this in Q4 2025, Fogel declined to give a number and Steenbergen pivoted to supply listings (8.6 million, up 8%) rather than room nights. |
| Flights are bringing in new customers and growing fast | Throughout | Air-ticket growth 45% (Q1 2025) → 44% → 32% → 37% for full-year 2025 → **4% (Q2 2026)**. | **Diverges, with a credible explanation.** Steenbergen attributes it to airline capacity cuts and higher fares from the Middle East conflict, and notes bookings value still grew about 12%. The explanation is plausible and externally verifiable. But the company also cut its full-year gross-bookings expectation specifically because of it. |
| "We aim to grow our top line metrics faster than marketing investments" | Q2 2026 | Marketing expense **+11%** against gross bookings **+9%**. Management concedes it in the same breath: "are willing to lean in when we see positive long-term value." | **Diverges.** This is the single most important line in the quarter. The company paid more, proportionally, to hold its funnel. One quarter is not a trend. Two would be. |
| Free cash flow is strong | Q2 2026 | Trailing free cash flow $9.54B on $28.24B of revenue — a 33.8% conversion rate, and 88% of EBITDA. Capital spending is 1.1% of revenue. Cash earnings exceed accounting earnings (income quality 1.37x). | **Matches, emphatically.** This is elite cash conversion. |
| Buybacks are creating value | Q1/Q2 2026 | $7.4 billion repurchased in the first half of 2026 at an average of about $173 per share. Diluted share count 770 million in Q2 2026 against 815 million a year earlier — **down 5.6%**. | **Matches on execution, open on judgement.** The average price paid in the first half, $173, is *above* today's $170.32. They have not yet made money on this year's buying. |
| Returns on capital are exceptional | Implied | Return on invested capital **71%** on $6.87B of invested capital; operating return on assets 33.9%. Stock compensation is 2.1% of revenue. | **Matches.** For comparison, Airbnb runs 21% return on invested capital with stock compensation at 12.9% of revenue. |

**The one number that needs defusing.** The screener shows return on equity at −54% and the live data at −97%. This is not distress. Booking has bought back so much of itself that shareholders' equity is negative — tangible asset value of −$14.3 billion. Return on equity is arithmetically meaningless when the denominator is below zero. Return on invested capital, at 71%, is the number that describes this business. The same artefact explains why the screener's "Buffett fair value" of $375 and its earnings-power model reading of −100% are both unusable here: book-value-anchored models cannot process a company with no book value. Only the discounted-cash-flow reading of $230 sits in a sane range, and I have not leaned on any of them.

**The number that genuinely deserves a caution flag.** The screener reports "latest-quarter earnings per share up 131% year over year." That is true and misleading. The second quarter of 2025 carried a $1,146 million charge below the operating line that crushed reported net income to $895 million. Strip the comparison out and the honest growth number is the one management gave: adjusted earnings per share up **15%**, of which about six points came from the shrinking share count. Operating income grew 11%. Anyone underwriting on 131% is underwriting an accident.

---

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable, with the confidence migrating from the top line to the balance sheet.**

- **Q1 2025 — offensive.** "Things seem to be going pretty darn good." Fogel volunteers that agentic AI might be "wonderful for us."
- **Q2 2025 — offensive, and specific.** Steenbergen introduces his "double discipline" framework and gives exact figures: $150 million of savings taken out, $170 million reinvested. He also, against his own short-term interest, warns analysts off an easy fourth-quarter comparison: the prior year's strength was partly "relatively low comps… that is not so real." Executives who talk down their own forward optics are worth listening to.
- **Q3 2025 — confident but rhetorical.** The competitive-intensity answer is a history lecture. It is persuasive and it is unfalsifiable.
- **Q4 2025 — first defensive note.** The European regulatory recitation. Reinvestment rises to about $700 million gross, and Steenbergen pre-empts the margin question: net EBITDA impact about $300 million, offset by $250 million of in-year transformation savings, so "largely self-funded."
- **Q1 2026 — defensive framing, offensive capital allocation.** Fogel opens by acknowledging the Middle East conflict and immediately reaches for precedent: COVID, Ukraine, Israel-Hamas. Then pivots to the record $3.6 billion buyback and the $93 average purchase price. When the growth story gets harder to tell, the capital-return story gets louder. That is a rational response — but it is also a tell.
- **Q2 2026 — measured, and notably honest about the things that are going wrong.** The prepared remarks concede continued pressure on search-engine placement, marketing growing faster than bookings, and a reduced full-year gross-bookings expectation. Fogel's closing framing is the most sober of the six calls: "What gives us confidence is not the expectation that the world will become more predictable, rather, it is our confidence in our ability to execute."

**Guidance specificity increased rather than decreased** — the mark of a team that is not hiding. By the second quarter of 2026 they were quantifying the currency effect to the percentage point (about 1 point of drag in the third quarter, about 1.5 points of help for the full year on gross bookings), naming the euro assumption ($1.15), and sizing the war's impact quarter by quarter.

---

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.**

The pattern is consistent and verifiable across the window:

| Quarter | What they promised, and what landed |
|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | Room nights "slightly exceeded the high end"; revenue and EBITDA both "exceeded the high end." |
| Q2 2025 | Room nights, gross bookings and revenue all "above the high end." |
| Q3 2025 | All three metrics "above the high end of our prior guidance ranges." |
| Q4 2025 | Room nights "exceeded the high end." Full-year transformation savings of ~$550 million landed at "the high end of our prior guidance." |
| Q1 2026 | Room nights **"in line with our prior expectations"** — the one quarter in the window that did not beat. The Middle East conflict began at the end of February. |
| Q2 2026 | All four key metrics beat, room nights by about 1 point and gross bookings by about 3 points. |

**On sandbagging.** There is a mild, systematic conservatism here — the kind that produces a 7-for-7 beat record. It is not egregious: the guidance ranges are narrow and the beats are measured in single percentage points, not multiples. Crucially, management has twice acted against its own optics: talking down the fourth-quarter 2024 comparison in Q2 2025, and putting a specific two-percentage-point number on its own war headwind in Q1 2026 when a vaguer "macro pressure" would have served them better.

**The one guidance event that cuts the other way.** On 2026-08-04 the company **lowered** its full-year gross-bookings expectation — "primarily due to lower flight ticket growth, while our accommodation outlook remains largely unchanged." That is the first downward revision in the window. It is narrow, well-explained and confined to the smallest-margin vertical. It is still a cut.

---

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring non-answer is the one that matters most to the share price: quantify the AI benefit.**

Mark Mahaney asked it directly on 2026-08-04 — has Penny, after a year and a half, measurably improved conversion or bookings per customer? Fogel: "it's still very small, and we're not at a stage where we're going to start giving away percentages, numbers, increases in customer satisfaction or anything of that nature." Kevin Kopelman asked the same about the new discovery experience: "it's very early. I don't have any data to come back to you." Ron Josey asked in Q1 2026; the answer was "a very small sample."

Four separate analysts, three quarters, the same refusal. Management's position is internally consistent — they have a genuine policy of not disclosing test metrics, and Fogel's counter is a good one ("if it's still there, it means that it's doing something positive for us; every single pixel is very, very valuable"). But the market is currently repricing this company *entirely* on the AI question, and this is the single quantitative gap in an otherwise unusually well-quantified disclosure record.

**The second recurring pressure point is alternative accommodations.** Trevor Young pushed on decelerating growth in Q4 2025 and got a supply-listings answer instead of a room-nights answer. The metric has since decelerated further, to 4%.

**What analysts pushed on that later turned into bad news.** Ken Gawrelski asked in Q1 2025 about United States weakness and whether Booking could take share; management described the opportunity confidently. United States room-night growth then did accelerate for four consecutive quarters to low teens by Q1 2026 — and then fell back to high single digits in Q2 2026. The share gain was real; it was not permanent.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be.** Nobody on the second-quarter 2026 call asked why marketing expense grew 11% against 9% gross bookings. That is the number that would tell you whether the funnel is getting more expensive to defend.

---

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

1. **Five straight quarters of decelerating room nights** — 9% in Q4 2025 to 5% in Q2 2026, guided to 3–5% for Q3 2026. Some is the war; not all of it is.
2. **The flagship strategic metric has decelerated every quarter**, from 35% connected-trip transaction growth in Q1 2025 to low double digits in Q2 2026. Management reframes the denominator each time.
3. **Marketing grew faster than gross bookings in Q2 2026** (11% vs 9%). The first proportional concession on customer-acquisition cost in the window.
4. **Search-engine placement pressure is now conceded on the record** (Q2 2026): "continued pressure on SEO, which we're seeing across much of consumer Internet."
5. **Insider behaviour is one-directional.** Zero open-market purchases against 66 sales totalling 164,362 shares. Management buys this stock enthusiastically with the company's cash and not at all with its own.
6. **Negative tangible equity of −$14.3 billion.** Years of buybacks have consumed the balance sheet. This is a deliberate, rational choice for a business with 71% returns on capital and no need for assets — but it means there is no asset floor under the shares. None.
7. **A downward guidance revision on 2026-08-04**, the first of the window.
8. **The buyback is currently under water.** $7.4 billion deployed in the first half at an average of about $173, against $170.32 today.

**🟢 Green flags**

1. **Elite and *improving* unit economics.** Return on invested capital 71%. Capital spending 1.1% of revenue. Stock compensation 2.1% of revenue — one sixth of Airbnb's 12.9%. Cash earnings run 1.37x accounting earnings. Margins expanded in both years of the window.
2. **A 7-for-7 beat record**, delivered with narrow guidance ranges rather than wide ones.
3. **Management quantifies its own headwinds unprompted** — two percentage points from the war in Q1 2026, currency bridged to the point every quarter.
4. **The transformation programme is over-delivering.** Launched November 2024; $550 million of run-rate savings by the end of 2025 (the high end of guidance); **raised to approximately $650 million on 2026-08-04**, with the extra $100 million landing mostly in 2027.
5. **The lock-in metrics are still improving while growth slows** — a genuinely important divergence. Direct booking mix held stable in the mid-60% range with direct room nights still growing. Genius Level 2 and 3 members are more than 30% of the active base and now account for a *high* 50% share of room nights, up year over year. Merchant-of-record share of gross bookings reached 73%, **up four percentage points year over year**. The customers are getting stickier even as the cohort gets smaller.
6. **Artificial intelligence is already paying on the cost line.** Voice support is scaled across the majority of eligible inbound calls; customer-service cost per booking is falling at a double-digit rate.
7. **The disintermediation fear is measurably not showing up.** Traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid, is "significantly below 1% of our room nights" and "hasn't moved so much recently" (2026-08-04). Booking is inside the new channels, not outside them: a participant in OpenAI's cost-per-click test group and among the first partners in Google's agentic booking rollout.
8. **Unusual disclosure candour on capital allocation** — publishing the multi-year average buyback price of $93 and the half-year average of $173 is not required and is not flattering.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary moved from "competitive advantage" to "protect."** In Q1 2025, agentic AI was a possible source of cheaper customer acquisition. By Q2 2026, Steenbergen's framing is explicitly defensive: "it's very important to protect customers that are coming direct to us… so that they can have that experience, that full experience in our environment." He catches himself mid-sentence — "actually not protect the direct channel but further expand the direct channel" — which is the most revealing half-second in six calls.

**Fogel now volunteers Google as the precedent, not the threat.** In Q4 2025: "we've been competing, so to speak, with a top-of-the-funnel player who's very big for a very long time… They've made very good money setting up an auction format for taking advertising, and we have been more than happy to pay a lot of money." He then predicts the language-model companies will do the same — "take it high above, don't become a merchant of record." By Q2 2026 he claims that prediction as correct: "I thought that one of them would start going for a performance marketing advertising platform, which is right in our wheelhouse… and they have." This is the bull case and the bear case in one paragraph. If agents become an advertising auction, Booking wins — it is the best bidder in the world. If agents become the merchant of record, Booking loses the customer. Fogel is betting on the first, explicitly and on the record.

**A revealing asymmetry in the second-quarter 2026 AI disclosure.** Third-party data says Booking's brands *appear* frequently in language-model outputs, but "the referrals aren't showing much." Fogel's reading — "we hope it actually reminds people when they do get ready to book" — is a hope, and he labels it as one. Visibility without referral traffic is either latent brand value or a leak. Nobody knows yet, including him.

**Capital allocation is now the loudest signal management sends.** Retiring roughly $14–15 billion a year against a $132 billion market value is an implicit statement that management believes the shares are worth materially more than the tape. They paid $173 on average in the first half. They did not stop when the price fell.

**Continuity of voice.** Fogel (26 years at the company as of February 2026) and Steenbergen have presented every call in the window together. There are no new voices, no departures, no restatements, no auditor changes.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

Not strengthening — every disclosed volume metric has decelerated for five consecutive quarters, and the third-quarter guide of 3–5% room nights is the slowest in the window. Not deteriorating — margins are still expanding, the efficiency programme was raised rather than trimmed, cash conversion is elite and improving, and the stickiness metrics (direct mix, Genius share of room nights, merchant-of-record share) all moved the right way in the same quarter that growth slowed.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** You are not underwriting Booking's earnings power; that is visible, high-quality and well disclosed. You are underwriting **one unresolved question: whether artificial-intelligence agents become an advertising auction that Booking wins, or a booking layer that routes around it.** Management has taken a public, specific position on that question and is backing it with roughly $14–15 billion a year of its own buying. The evidence available today supports them — under 1% of room nights come via language models and that share is not moving, while direct mix holds and merchant-of-record share climbs. But the evidence is *early*, and management has declined four times to quantify the one metric that would settle it.

Size to the fact that this question will not be answered inside a quarter. It will be answered over years, by the product decisions of two or three companies that are not Booking.

**Economic moat: WIDE. Moat trend: STABLE.**

The moat type is a **two-sided network with switching costs layered on top**. The network: roughly 31 million accommodation listings, including 8.6 million alternative-accommodation listings, against hundreds of millions of travellers — neither side can be replicated without the other. The switching costs are the newer and more interesting part: Genius members in the top two tiers now account for a high 50% share of room nights and book more often, cancel less and book further ahead; the merchant-of-record share at 73% means Booking holds the payment relationship, the service obligation and the refund liability, which is exactly the messy, regulated, capital-consuming work Fogel argues language models will not want.

**The width judgement rests on the returns evidence, and that evidence points one way.** Return on invested capital is 71% and has not fallen. Operating return on assets is 33.9%. Adjusted margins expanded 193 basis points in 2025 and roughly 40 more basis points in the second quarter of 2026. Capital intensity is 1.1% of revenue, stock compensation 2.1%. This is the opposite of an eroding moat, where you would expect falling returns and margin defended by cuts. Here returns are flat-to-up and the margin is funded by a savings programme management keeps *raising*.

**The trend is stable rather than widening**, and that distinction is deliberate. Three things prevent a widening call: marketing spend grew faster than gross bookings for the first time in the window; search-engine placement pressure is conceded on the record; and the flagship connected-trip metric has decelerated from 35% to low double digits over six quarters. The fortress walls are not falling. They are being tested, and the company has started paying a little more to hold them.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The relevant structural force is generative-AI displacement — the same force that is the book's largest concentration. The honest case that it is terminal: if a traveller's entire journey happens inside an assistant that holds the payment credential and the itinerary, the online travel agency becomes a wholesale inventory supplier with a wholesale margin. The honest case that it is not: that requires the assistant's owner to become a merchant of record in more than 200 jurisdictions, absorb refund liability, staff customer service, and comply with the European regulatory stack Fogel enumerates — a business with 1% capital intensity today becoming one with real liabilities. The observable data currently favours the second reading: language-model traffic is below 1% of room nights and flat, the direct channel is stable, and Booking is a launch partner inside both of the channels people fear.

**Fear-print or value trap?** On the evidence, a **fear print**. A value trap is a low multiple on a *shrinking* base with *falling* returns. Booking's base is still growing — slower, but growing — its returns are not falling, its margins are expanding, and its cash conversion is improving. What has fallen is the multiple the market will pay for that base. That is a change in perception, not in the machine. The qualifier is that a fear print is only a mispricing if the fear is wrong, and this particular fear will take years to settle. Do not size it as though a single quarter can resolve it.

Management credibility 4 of 5 · trajectory steady · a wide, durable moat · moat trend steady · structural threat material.

bull_thesis: The bull case is that the market has repriced a fear and not a fact, and that the company is quietly buying the difference. Start with what the machine actually does. Booking turned $28.2 billion of trailing revenue into $9.54 billion of free cash - a 34% conversion rate, and 88% of its own earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. It does this on capital spending of 1.1% of revenue and stock-based compensation of 2.1% of revenue, which is one sixth of Airbnb's 12.9%. Return on invested capital is 71%. Cash earnings run 1.37 times accounting earnings. Very few businesses of this scale anywhere convert like this, and none of the listed travel peers do. The fear is that artificial-intelligence assistants will stand between Booking and the traveller. On the evidence management put on the record on 2026-08-04, that is not happening yet and is not trending: traffic reaching Booking from large language models, paid and unpaid combined, is 'significantly below 1% of our room nights' and 'hasn't moved so much recently'. Meanwhile the three metrics that measure whether customers are getting stickier all improved in that same quarter - the share of bookings taken directly rather than through paid channels held stable in the mid-60% range with direct volumes still growing; members of the top two loyalty tiers rose to a high-50% share of all room nights; and the share of gross bookings where Booking is the merchant of record, holding the payment and the service obligation, reached 73%, up four percentage points in a year. Customers are getting stickier while the market prices them getting looser. Second, Booking is inside the new channels rather than outside them: it is in OpenAI's cost-per-click test group and among the first partners in Google's agentic booking rollout. The chief executive's public bet, stated plainly on the fourth-quarter 2025 call, is that assistant owners will do what Google did - build an advertising auction above the funnel and decline the regulated, refund-bearing, 200-jurisdiction work of being a merchant of record. If he is right, Booking is the best bidder in the world in that auction and the fear inverts into a cheaper customer-acquisition channel. Third, artificial intelligence is already earning its keep on the cost line, not the revenue line: voice support now covers the majority of eligible inbound traveller calls and customer-service cost per booking is falling at a double-digit rate, while the efficiency programme's expected annual savings were raised from about $550 million to about $650 million on 2026-08-04. Fourth, and most concretely, the company is retiring roughly $14-15 billion of its own stock a year against a $132 billion market value - about 11% of the shares outstanding annually. It bought $7.4 billion in the first half of 2026 at an average of about $173 per share, above today's $170.32, and did not stop when the price fell. Diluted share count is down 5.6% in a year. At an unchanged multiple, that alone compounds per-share value at high single digits. Fifth, the management record supports taking their word on the things they cannot yet prove: seven earnings beats in seven quarters against narrow guidance ranges, a war headwind they sized themselves at two percentage points rather than leaving vague, a currency effect bridged to the point every quarter, and an unprompted disclosure of the multi-year average buyback price of $93 per share. The conditions the bull case requires are specific and checkable: language-model referral share must stay under a low-single-digit percentage of room nights; the direct booking mix must hold in the mid-60s; marketing spend must stop growing faster than gross bookings; and room-night growth must stabilise at or above the top of the 3-5% guided range once the Middle East corridor pressure fades.
bear_thesis: The bear case does not need the disintermediation fear to be right. It only needs growth to keep slowing while the balance sheet has nothing left underneath it. Look at the volume record across six consecutive calls. Room nights: 7%, then 8%, 8%, 9%, 6%, and 5% in the second quarter of 2026, with third-quarter guidance of 3-5% - the slowest in the window. To be exact about the second quarter itself: those prints beat the high end of the company's own guidance, room nights by about a percentage point and gross bookings by about three, so the deceleration is a trend in the level, not a miss against the bar. The flagship strategic metric, connected-trip transactions where a traveller books more than one part of a journey, has decelerated in every single quarter without exception, from 35% growth in the first quarter of 2025 to low double digits in the second quarter of 2026; management reframes the denominator each time rather than address the line. Alternative accommodations, long sold as a structural growth engine, grew 4% in the latest quarter - slower than the company as a whole, after 12% eighteen months earlier. Flight tickets went from 45% growth to 4%. On 2026-08-04 the company cut its full-year gross-bookings expectation for the first time in the record - and the cut has to be stated with the cause management gave it, which is flights and war rather than the profit engine: 'primarily due to lower flight ticket growth, while our accommodation outlook remains largely unchanged', with the full-year guide still in line with the original on a constant-currency basis despite carrying seven of twelve months of Middle East impact. On 2026-09-09 the European General Court upheld the veto of its $1.9 billion purchase of eTraveli, permanently shutting the acquisition route into flights. The single most important line in the last quarter went unchallenged by every analyst on the call: marketing expense grew 11% against gross bookings of 9% - $2,371 million against $2,139 million a year earlier. We had called that the first proportional concession on the cost of acquiring a customer in the whole window. It is not the first, and correcting the count makes the bear case older rather than weaker: in the first quarter of 2026 marketing expense was $2,068 million against $1,777 million, up 16.4%, against reported gross bookings up 15%. The cost of buying the volume already outgrew the volume a full quarter earlier, on both the reported and the constant-currency reading. So the second quarter is the second consecutive quarter of it, and it arrives in the same quarter management conceded 'continued pressure on SEO' - the free traffic that search engines used to deliver. If assistants are going to hurt, this is the shape the damage takes first: not a collapse in volume but a steady, grinding rise in what it costs to buy the same volume. One quarter is noise and two is a trend, so the trend clock has already run; what prints in late October is the third test of it, which is why that report either establishes the toll or breaks it. Second, there is no floor here. Years of buybacks have taken shareholders' equity negative - tangible asset value of minus $14.3 billion. There are no assets to liquidate, no net cash to fall back on, no announced distribution, no deal terms. The 0.84% dividend is not a floor. The correct statement of downside is: whatever multiple a frightened market will pay for the cash flows, times the cash flows. That is it. Net debt is $3.48 billion including capitalised leases, against $20.18 billion of borrowings and $17.21 billion of cash, so the apparent cash pile is not spare - it is matched by debt. Third, the buyback itself is a risk disguised as a virtue. The company spent $7.4 billion in the first half of 2026 at an average of about $173 per share to buy a stock now at $170.32. It is down on this year's purchases. If the growth rate settles at 3-4% rather than 8%, management will have retired roughly a tenth of the company each year at prices set by a multiple that was still de-rating. Fourth, insiders vote the other way with their own money: zero open-market purchases against 66 sales totalling 164,362 shares. Fifth, the macro backdrop turned hostile after the last look. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 2026-09-16 in a unanimous vote with sixteen of eighteen policymakers pointing to another increase; the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007; Brent crude peaked at a $108.75 close on 2026-09-15; and consumer sentiment sits at 47.8. Travel is the most deferrable large item in a household budget. Management has already told us the Middle East corridor will keep suppressing long-haul demand and inflating flight prices through the third quarter. Sixth, the disintermediation risk is real even if it is slow, and its form is take-rate compression rather than lost volume: if assistants become the demand layer, Booking pays a new toll on top of the one it already pays Google, and the 34% free-cash margin is exactly the fat that toll would come out of. What would confirm the bear case: marketing growing faster than gross bookings for a third consecutive quarter in late October; the direct booking mix slipping out of the mid-60% range; language-model referral share moving off its sub-1% base in either direction with no matching revenue; or a fourth-quarter guide with room nights below 3%.
consensus_delta: We disagree with both sides of this argument, which is unusual and worth stating plainly. Wall Street's published target is $233.30, with a median of $237 and a range of $188 to $270. That number has barely moved all year: the average target over the last twelve months is $232.70, over the last quarter $231.00, and over the last month $229.33 - while the shares fell about 22% year to date and the company itself cut its full-year gross-bookings expectation on 2026-08-04. Analysts have marked their opinions to the calendar, not to the disclosures. The specific assumption embedded in a $233 target is a return to something like the 8% room-night growth of 2025 on a multiple near twenty times cash flow. Management has just guided third-quarter room nights to 3-5% and told us the pressure on long-haul travel persists through the quarter. So our first disagreement is that the Street's anchor is too high and too stale, and we sit below it at $204. Our second disagreement runs the other way and is the more interesting one. The market has taken the shares from $209.62 on 2026-08-21 to $167.90 on 2026-09-18, a fall of about 20% in under a month, on the proposition that artificial-intelligence assistants are dismantling the online travel agent. The company's own disclosure on 2026-08-04 is that traffic arriving from large language models, paid and unpaid combined, is 'significantly below 1% of our room nights' and 'hasn't moved so much recently' - while the three measures of customer stickiness all improved in the same quarter: the direct booking mix held in the mid-60% range with volumes still growing, top-tier loyalty members rose to a high-50% share of room nights, and the share of bookings where Booking holds the payment and the service obligation reached 73%, up four points in a year. A business being disintermediated does not tighten its grip on its customers while it is being disintermediated. Both disagreements can be true at once: the Street's number is wrong and the market's fear is running ahead of the evidence. Our $204 sits between them on purpose. The one place we side with the bears against the Street is the thing nobody asked about on the last call: marketing spend grew 11% against gross bookings of 9%. If the toll on acquiring a customer is rising, that is where it shows up first, and it is the number we will be checking before we upgrade.
forcing_function: There is no single event that forces this re-rating, and saying otherwise would be inventing one. Three things could do it, in descending order of how dated they are. First and most concrete: the third-quarter report, which the screener places about 36 days out and which the company has delivered in the last week of October in each of the last two years - we have not confirmed the 2026 date directly. That print carries the two numbers that settle the argument for the next six months: whether room nights land at or above the top of the guided 3-5%, and whether marketing spend stops growing faster than gross bookings. A clean answer on both, with the direct booking mix still in the mid-60% range, would break the disintermediation narrative in the only way narratives ever break - by failing to show up in the numbers for a third consecutive quarter. Second, and undated but continuous: the buyback. At roughly 11% of the shares a year, share-count reduction alone lifts per-share earnings at high single digits before the business grows at all; if the multiple merely stops falling, the arithmetic does the rest. Management's own revealed view of value is on the record - an average of $93 per share since 2014 and about $173 in the first half of 2026 - and they did not stop when the price fell. Third, and the real prize, is the one nobody controls: a public commitment from Google or OpenAI to an advertising-auction model rather than a merchant-of-record model for travel. Booking is already inside both - a participant in OpenAI's cost-per-click test and among the first partners in Google's agentic booking rollout - and the chief executive has staked his public argument on that outcome. That resolution has no date and may arrive in fragments over years. What is now definitively off the table: the eTraveli acquisition, vetoed by the European Commission and upheld by the European General Court on 2026-09-09.
valley_of_death: There is no cash crisis in the next three to nine months - this company generated $9.54 billion of free cash over the last twelve months on capital spending of 1.1% of revenue, holds $17.2 billion of cash and investments, and carries net debt of only about a third of one year's profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. The risk is entirely to the multiple, and it has four distinct sources stacked in a short window. First, the growth print itself. Third-quarter guidance of 3-5% room nights is the slowest in two years, and the third-quarter report - due in the last week of October if the company keeps to its recent pattern - is the first chance for that number to disappoint against an already-lowered bar. Management has pre-committed to the Middle East corridor continuing to suppress long-haul demand and inflate flight prices through the quarter, which removes the excuse but not the damage. Second, and more dangerous for the thesis, the marketing line. Spend grew 11% against 9% gross bookings in the second quarter. A second consecutive quarter of that in late October would convert a one-off into the first hard evidence that the cost of holding the funnel is structurally rising, and would take the shares below our adverse case rather than to it. Third, the macro backdrop turned genuinely hostile in the last ten days. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 2026-09-16 by a quarter point to 3.75-4.00% in a unanimous vote, with sixteen of eighteen policymakers pointing to another increase; the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007; Brent crude peaked at a $108.75 close on 2026-09-15 before easing near $100; and consumer sentiment sits at 47.8. Travel is the most deferrable large item in a household budget, and it is being squeezed from both ends at once - the consumer's income and the airline's fuel bill. Fourth, headline risk from the assistant narrative is continuous and unpredictable, as 2026-09-08's single-day fall of 6.7% demonstrated. A product announcement from Google or OpenAI that looks like a booking layer rather than an advertising layer would hit this stock before anyone could measure whether it mattered. The offsetting force, and it is a real one, is that the company is buying roughly $3.5-4 billion of its own stock every quarter into exactly this weakness.
positioning_washout: The mechanics here run the opposite way to the usual forced-selling story, which is precisely why we are not yet buying. There is no dividend cut in prospect and no income-focused shareholder base to flush - the yield is 0.84%, a rounding error. The largest mechanical participant in this stock is the company itself, retiring roughly $14-15 billion a year, about 11% of the shares outstanding, and it has not flinched: $7.4 billion in the first half of 2026 at an average of about $173 per share, above today's $170.32. That is a permanent, price-insensitive bid, and it means the classic capitulation - where the marginal seller runs out and the stock gaps - is partly pre-empted. Institutions were still adding through the second quarter, with First Eagle taking an $876 million new position and BlackRock at 8.70%. So where is the selling pressure? It is in momentum and quality-growth mandates, not in income. The shares sit about 24% below their 52-week high of $225.00, below both their 50-day average of $192.78 and their 200-day average of $184.78, and only 25% up their 52-week range. Screens that rank on trailing twelve-month price will be dropping this name into year-end, and the December quarter brings the usual window-dressing pressure on a stock that has been a visible loser. Retail is already defensive: the American Association of Individual Investors reported 28.8% bulls against 53.3% bears on 2026-09-17. But - and this is the point that decides our verdict - none of that has produced a washout. The fall from $209.62 on 2026-08-21 to $167.90 on 2026-09-18 was a steady grind, not a flush; the highest closing volatility reading in that whole window was 17.84, which is not panic. Options activity on 2026-09-21 ran roughly ten times normal volume with attention on the October $150 puts, which tells you the market is positioning for a lower low rather than covering. A stock that has de-rated 20% without a capitulation print usually has one more leg in it. The 52-week low of $150.14 is 12% away.
moderator_conclusion: This is a wide-moat business at a fair price rather than a wonderful one, and the distinction is what keeps it on the watchlist rather than in the book. Start with what is not in doubt. Booking converts 34% of revenue into free cash, earns 71% on invested capital, spends 1.1% of revenue on capital and 2.1% on stock compensation, has beaten the high end of its own guidance in seven consecutive quarters, and raised its efficiency programme's expected annual savings from about $550 million to about $650 million on 2026-08-04. The management team quantifies its own headwinds unprompted, bridges its currency benefit every quarter, and publishes the average price it pays for its own stock. On forensics this is close to a clean sheet, and we score management credibility at four out of five, marked down one notch only because they have now declined four times, across three quarters and four different analysts, to quantify the one thing the market most wants measured: whether their artificial-intelligence tools improve conversion. Now the harder half. Every volume metric this company discloses has decelerated for five straight quarters. Room nights went 9% to 5% and are guided to 3-5%. The flagship connected-trip metric went from 35% growth to low double digits without a single quarter's interruption. Alternative accommodations, long sold as the growth engine, grew 4% - slower than the company. That deceleration is in the level and not against the bar: room nights, gross bookings, revenue and adjusted profit all beat the high end of guidance in the second quarter, room nights by about a point and gross bookings by about three. On 2026-08-04 the full-year gross-bookings expectation came down for the first time in the record - on lower flight-ticket growth, with the accommodation outlook largely unchanged and the full-year guide still in line with the original at constant currency, so it is a flights-and-war cut rather than a verdict on the profit engine. On 2026-09-09 a European court permanently closed the acquisition route into flights. And in the same quarter, marketing spend grew 11% against gross bookings of 9% - a proportional concession on the cost of buying a customer, arriving alongside a conceded deterioration in free search traffic. We had called it the first such quarter in the window and it was not: the first quarter of 2026 already ran marketing up 16.4% ($2,068 million against $1,777 million) against reported gross bookings up 15%. That is the shape assistant pressure would take if it were real - not lost volume, but a rising toll - and it has now printed twice in a row rather than once. What lands in late October is the third test of it, not the second, which makes that report the one that either establishes the toll or breaks it. On the central question we side with the company over the market, but with a time horizon the market does not have. Language-model traffic is under 1% of room nights and flat, while the direct booking mix, the loyalty share of room nights and the merchant-of-record share of bookings all improved in the same quarter - a business being routed around does not tighten its grip on its customers while it happens. We therefore read the de-rating as a fear print rather than a value trap: a low multiple on a growing base with rising returns, not a low multiple on a melting one. But this fear cannot be resolved inside a quarter. It will be settled over years, by product decisions at two or three companies that are not Booking, and anyone sizing this as a six-month trade is mispricing the clock. Which brings us to why we wait. Our sum-of-the-parts base case is $204, marked down from the $220 we carried last time because the bookings guide came down and the flights acquisition route is now closed by a court. At $170.32 that is 19.8% of upside - real, but short of this book's 20% entry floor, and not the kind of gap that pays you for an unresolved terminal question in a tightening-rate, hostile-consumer tape. Against it sits an adverse case of $145 rather than the $136 we first carried. The adverse build had divided its unchanged $105.8 billion of equity value by about 780 million shares on the stated premise that the buyback merely slows, when 770 million was the weighted-average diluted count in the second quarter and roughly 759 million were outstanding at 30 June; even a severely slowed programme leaves about 730 million, so the adverse case is $145 and the downside is 14.9%, for reward to risk of 1.33 to one against the 0.98 the record was graded on. That splits this book's two tests for the first time in this name: reward to risk now clears the one-for-one bar, while the discount still fails the 20% floor - and the discount is the test this stance was built on, because base fair value did not move and the correction cut the divisor, not the price we think the business is worth. So the grade is reviewed and held rather than re-rolled, the more so because the other correction runs against us: the rising cost of buying a customer turns out to be a quarter older than we said, not a quarter younger. What has not changed at all is that there is nothing structural underneath: tangible asset value is minus $14.3 billion, net debt is $3.48 billion, and there is no net cash, no deal terms and no asset floor. When the only thing beneath a stock is the multiple a frightened market will pay, you buy after the fright and not during it - and the fright has not finished. The fall from $209.62 on 2026-08-21 to $167.90 on 2026-09-18 was a steady grind, not a capitulation: the highest closing volatility print in that window was 17.84, and the options market spent 2026-09-21 positioning for a lower low. The 52-week low of $150.14 is 12% away. So: wait, and be specific about what we are waiting for. We will buy this on either of two developments. Either the price reaches the $150-155 zone - the 52-week low area, which would put the shares near 12.5 times free cash flow and roughly a third below our fair value, a discount wide enough to be paid for the terminal uncertainty. Or the third-quarter report, expected in the last week of October, delivers room nights at or above the top of the 3-5% guided range with marketing spend no longer outgrowing gross bookings and the direct mix holding in the mid-60s - at which point the narrative has failed its third consecutive test and we pay up without waiting for the price. One of those two will happen inside six months. On the value case judged alone, ignoring the spent catalyst and the macro tilt entirely, this is a four out of five: an elite-returning, clean-forensic franchise at roughly a fifth below fair value, with the company itself retiring a tenth of the shares a year above today's price. The single ingredient withholding the top mark is the size of the discount, not the quality of the business. On execution timing, with a hiking Federal Reserve, a ten-year Treasury at 5%, oil near $100 and the most deferrable category in consumer spending, it is a hold and a watch. Finally, a sizing note for the director: this name carries the generative-artificial-intelligence displacement theme, which is already the book's largest structural concentration. Its wide, non-eroding moat means it should count at half weight against that budget under the concentration rule - but it should count.
sop_breakdown: Base case, valuing the three disclosed revenue engines separately and then netting debt. Trailing earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation are $10.79 billion, allocated by revenue share with a modest quality tilt toward the merchant and advertising lines. (1) Merchant engine - Booking takes the payment and carries the service and refund obligation; 66% of revenue, 73% of gross bookings and rising; roughly $7.34 billion of profit at 17 times = $124.7 billion. The multiple is the judgement call: Airbnb trades at 31.6 times profit today and Expedia at 8.1 times, and this is the part of Booking that most resembles Airbnb on economics and least resembles Expedia. (2) Agency engine - commission on a referral, no payment relationship, the leg genuinely exposed to assistants and to search-engine decay; 30% of revenue, roughly $2.91 billion of profit at 10 times = $29.1 billion, valued close to Expedia's multiple because that is the honest comparison for a pure-referral business. (3) Advertising and the smaller brands (Kayak, OpenTable); about 4% of revenue, roughly $0.54 billion of profit at 13 times = $7.0 billion. Enterprise value $160.8 billion. Subtract net debt of $3.48 billion - $20.18 billion of borrowings plus $0.51 billion of capitalised leases, less $17.21 billion of cash; this is a liability and we subtract it rather than adding cash back, and we use the lease-inclusive definition rather than the $2.97 billion the filings often quote. Equity value $157.4 billion over 770 million diluted shares = $204 per share. Sanity check against the whole company: that is about 14.9 times profit and 16.9 times free cash flow, against 12.5 and 14.2 times at today's price - a fair value that asks for roughly a fifth more than the tape, not a doubling. We have deliberately not used the screener's model stack here. Its $375 Buffett-style fair value and its minus-100% earnings-power reading are both artefacts of a company with negative book equity, which book-anchored models cannot process; only the $230 discounted-cash-flow reading is in a sane range, and we did not lean on it either.
risk_reward: Modestly favourable rather than symmetric, and on the corrected arithmetic the asymmetry now sits in the numbers as well as in the favourable leg. From $170.32, our base case is $204 - about a fifth up - and our adverse case is $145, about 15% down: reward to risk of 1.33 to one, where the uncorrected record read 0.98. The adverse case moved because its divisor was wrong, not because the scenario softened. It divided an unchanged $105.8 billion of adverse equity value by about 780 million diluted shares on its own stated premise that the buyback merely 'slows', when the weighted-average diluted count was 770 million in the second quarter of 2026 against 815 million a year earlier, management put the reduction at 6% on the 2026-08-04 call, and roughly 759 million shares were outstanding at 30 June 2026; even a severely slowed programme leaves about 730 million, which is $145 a share. The favourable case at $266 is where the payoff lives, and it requires the assistant fear to fail publicly over several quarters rather than at any single event. Two things keep this a wait rather than a buy even so. First, the upside did not move: base fair value is still $204 and the discount to it is still 19.8%, which does not clear this book's 20% entry floor. The correction improved the downside, not the case for paying today's price. Second, there is still no structural floor to lean on: tangible asset value is minus $14.3 billion, there is no net cash (net debt is $3.48 billion), no deal terms, no tender and no announced distribution, and the 0.84% dividend yield is not a floor. What the corrected adverse case does say is that the scenario lands at $145 - within a few dollars of the $150-155 zone at which we have already committed to buy - so the ground between here and the bad case is closer to our own entry than to a broken thesis. That is why we wait for the price rather than pay up for a franchise we like: when the only thing under a stock is the multiple a frightened market will pay, you want to buy after the fright, not during it.
catalyst_status_plain: a soft catalyst, no fixed date
peer_comps_note: We have replaced the supplied peer note's multiples with live ones, because the supplied note is wrong in a way that would have flattered this name. It states that Booking's 15 times free cash flow is 'roughly in line with or modestly cheap' against Airbnb and Expedia, which 'often trade in a similar-to-higher range'. On today's figures Expedia trades at 6.3 times enterprise value to free cash flow and 8.1 times profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation - less than half Booking's 14.2 and 12.5 times. Booking is not cheap against Expedia; it is at a large premium, and a premium it earns, since Expedia produces a 26% return on invested capital against Booking's 71%, carries more debt and is growing more slowly. Airbnb is the multiple that supports the case: 19.6 times free cash flow and 31.6 times profit, and that headline understates the gap because Airbnb charges 12.9% of revenue to stock-based compensation against Booking's 2.1%. Deduct that non-cash pay from both and Airbnb trades near 30 times cash generation while Booking trades near 15 - half the multiple for three times the return on capital and a fraction of the dilution. That is the one genuinely defensible relative-value lever here, and it is what sets the 17-times multiple on the merchant engine in our parts valuation. One important qualification, and it is the reason we do not credit the full gap as company-specific edge: the whole online travel cohort is de-rating together on the same unresolved question - whether assistants route around booking platforms. Booking's discount to its own history is therefore largely shared-sector movement on a single unresolved driver, not an idiosyncratic mispricing of this company alone. Treat the gap to Airbnb as a quality-adjusted relative-value observation, not as isolated alpha in this name.
interrogator_dossier:
# Booking Holdings (BKNG) — Forensic Interrogator Dossier
*Six consecutive earnings calls, 2025-04-29 through 2026-08-04, cross-referenced against the reported financials. Price used throughout: $170.32 per share (Nasdaq, in US dollars, live quote as of 2026-09-22). Note the company completed a 25-for-1 stock split on 2026-04-06, so all per-share figures here are on the post-split basis.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

**The story did not change. The numbers underneath it did.**

Across six calls, Glenn Fogel and Ewout Steenbergen told one continuous story with four pillars: the Connected Trip (getting a traveller to book more than one thing — a room plus a flight plus a car — in a single place), the Genius loyalty programme, geographic expansion into the United States and Asia, and artificial intelligence. Not one pillar was introduced and quietly dropped. Not one was renamed. That is rarer than it sounds, and it is a genuine credibility marker.

What *did* change is the emphasis and the arithmetic.

**Early in the window (first half of 2025), the tone was offensive.** The first-quarter 2025 call led with a record — "the first quarter we have ever exceeded 300 million room nights" — and the AI discussion was almost entirely about *opportunity*: smart filters, review summaries, a partner assistant. When an analyst raised agentic AI as a threat, Fogel's answer was expansive and almost gleeful: "Maybe what will happen is we'll end up with a whole bunch of them, which is going to be a lot more supply for new customers to be coming, which will lower the cost for us to acquire them. That could be wonderful for us."

**By the third-quarter 2025 call, the framing shifted from opportunity to positioning.** Asked directly by Trevor Young of Barclays whether competitive intensity would pick up over two to three years, Fogel answered with history rather than numbers — a recitation of TripAdvisor, of Meta, of mobile — closing with "I actually see us in a much better position than we were years ago, decades ago." That is a confident answer. It is not a quantified one.

**By the fourth-quarter 2025 call, a defensive edge appeared for the first time.** Fogel walked through the European regulatory alphabet unprompted — "you got DSA, DMA, DFA, EU, AIA, P2B, DAC7, I can go on and on, and that's just the EU" — to argue that large language models will not come down the funnel to where Booking operates. The argument is a good one. But the fact that it needed making, at length, without being asked in those terms, marks the point where the AI question stopped being a growth story and became a defence.

**By the second-quarter 2026 call (2026-08-04), the company was leading with AI as a strategic priority in its own right** — a full section of prepared remarks about working "closely with leading AI organizations to ensure travellers can engage with our brands wherever their journey begins." The most important disclosure of the entire six-call window sits in the Q&A of that call, from Steenbergen: traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid combined, is "still significantly below 1% of our room nights. And that hasn't moved so much recently."

**A second, quieter arc runs underneath: a war arrived and stayed.** The Middle East conflict began at the end of February 2026. It cost roughly two percentage points of room-night and gross-bookings growth in the first quarter of 2026, "a bit higher" in the second quarter, and is assumed to keep pressuring flight prices and long-haul capacity through the third quarter. Management's full-year guidance now embeds seven of twelve months of that impact.

**A third arc is capital allocation, and it became the loudest voice on the call.** Buybacks moved from a footnote to a headline. In the first quarter of 2026 the company repurchased a record $3.6 billion; in the second quarter, $3.7 billion, with $4.1 billion of total shareholder returns. Fogel put an unusual number on the record: share count down more than 40% since 2014, at an average purchase price of $93 per share.

---

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "We exceeded the high end of our guidance across all of our key financial metrics" | Q2 2026 | Revenue $7.35B, adjusted EBITDA ~$2.6B, adjusted earnings per share $2.54. The screener records seven earnings beats in seven quarters. | **Matches.** The beat pattern is real and unbroken. |

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rating: Stable, with the confidence migrating from the top line to the balance sheet.**

- **Q1 2025 — offensive.** "Things seem to be going pretty darn good." Fogel volunteers that agentic AI might be "wonderful for us."
- **Q2 2025 — offensive, and specific.** Steenbergen introduces his "double discipline" framework and gives exact figures: $150 million of savings taken out, $170 million reinvested. He also, against his own short-term interest, warns analysts off an easy fourth-quarter comparison: the prior year's strength was partly "relatively low comps… that is not so real." Executives who talk down their own forward optics are worth listening to.
- **Q3 2025 — confident but rhetorical.** The competitive-intensity answer is a history lecture. It is persuasive and it is unfalsifiable.
- **Q4 2025 — first defensive note.** The European regulatory recitation. Reinvestment rises to about $700 million gross, and Steenbergen pre-empts the margin question: net EBITDA impact about $300 million, offset by $250 million of in-year transformation savings, so "largely self-funded."
- **Q1 2026 — defensive framing, offensive capital allocation.** Fogel opens by acknowledging the Middle East conflict and immediately reaches for precedent: COVID, Ukraine, Israel-Hamas. Then pivots to the record $3.6 billion buyback and the $93 average purchase price. When the growth story gets harder to tell, the capital-return story gets louder. That is a rational response — but it is also a tell.
- **Q2 2026 — measured, and notably honest about the things that are going wrong.** The prepared remarks concede continued pressure on search-engine placement, marketing growing faster than bookings, and a reduced full-year gross-bookings expectation. Fogel's closing framing is the most sober of the six calls: "What gives us confidence is not the expectation that the world will become more predictable, rather, it is our confidence in our ability to execute."

**Guidance specificity increased rather than decreased** — the mark of a team that is not hiding. By the second quarter of 2026 they were quantifying the currency effect to the percentage point (about 1 point of drag in the third quarter, about 1.5 points of help for the full year on gross bookings), naming the euro assumption ($1.15), and sizing the war's impact quarter by quarter.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.**

The pattern is consistent and verifiable across the window:

| Quarter | What they promised, and what landed |
|---|---|
| Q1 2025 | Room nights "slightly exceeded the high end"; revenue and EBITDA both "exceeded the high end." |
| Q2 2025 | Room nights, gross bookings and revenue all "above the high end." |
| Q3 2025 | All three metrics "above the high end of our prior guidance ranges." |
| Q4 2025 | Room nights "exceeded the high end." Full-year transformation savings of ~$550 million landed at "the high end of our prior guidance." |
| Q1 2026 | Room nights **"in line with our prior expectations"** — the one quarter in the window that did not beat. The Middle East conflict began at the end of February. |
| Q2 2026 | All four key metrics beat, room nights by about 1 point and gross bookings by about 3 points. |

**On sandbagging.** There is a mild, systematic conservatism here — the kind that produces a 7-for-7 beat record. It is not egregious: the guidance ranges are narrow and the beats are measured in single percentage points, not multiples. Crucially, management has twice acted against its own optics: talking down the fourth-quarter 2024 comparison in Q2 2025, and putting a specific two-percentage-point number on its own war headwind in Q1 2026 when a vaguer "macro pressure" would have served them better.

**The one guidance event that cuts the other way.** On 2026-08-04 the company **lowered** its full-year gross-bookings expectation — "primarily due to lower flight ticket growth, while our accommodation outlook remains largely unchanged." That is the first downward revision in the window. It is narrow, well-explained and confined to the smallest-margin vertical. It is still a cut.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

**The recurring non-answer is the one that matters most to the share price: quantify the AI benefit.**

Mark Mahaney asked it directly on 2026-08-04 — has Penny, after a year and a half, measurably improved conversion or bookings per customer? Fogel: "it's still very small, and we're not at a stage where we're going to start giving away percentages, numbers, increases in customer satisfaction or anything of that nature." Kevin Kopelman asked the same about the new discovery experience: "it's very early. I don't have any data to come back to you." Ron Josey asked in Q1 2026; the answer was "a very small sample."

Four separate analysts, three quarters, the same refusal. Management's position is internally consistent — they have a genuine policy of not disclosing test metrics, and Fogel's counter is a good one ("if it's still there, it means that it's doing something positive for us; every single pixel is very, very valuable"). But the market is currently repricing this company *entirely* on the AI question, and this is the single quantitative gap in an otherwise unusually well-quantified disclosure record.

**The second recurring pressure point is alternative accommodations.** Trevor Young pushed on decelerating growth in Q4 2025 and got a supply-listings answer instead of a room-nights answer. The metric has since decelerated further, to 4%.

**What analysts pushed on that later turned into bad news.** Ken Gawrelski asked in Q1 2025 about United States weakness and whether Booking could take share; management described the opportunity confidently. United States room-night growth then did accelerate for four consecutive quarters to low teens by Q1 2026 — and then fell back to high single digits in Q2 2026. The share gain was real; it was not permanent.

**What analysts are not pressing on, and should be.** Nobody on the second-quarter 2026 call asked why marketing expense grew 11% against 9% gross bookings. That is the number that would tell you whether the funnel is getting more expensive to defend.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**🔴 Red flags**

1. **Five straight quarters of decelerating room nights** — 9% in Q4 2025 to 5% in Q2 2026, guided to 3–5% for Q3 2026. Some is the war; not all of it is.
2. **The flagship strategic metric has decelerated every quarter**, from 35% connected-trip transaction growth in Q1 2025 to low double digits in Q2 2026. Management reframes the denominator each time.
3. **Marketing grew faster than gross bookings in Q2 2026** (11% vs 9%). The first proportional concession on customer-acquisition cost in the window.
4. **Search-engine placement pressure is now conceded on the record** (Q2 2026): "continued pressure on SEO, which we're seeing across much of consumer Internet."
5. **Insider behaviour is one-directional.** Zero open-market purchases against 66 sales totalling 164,362 shares. Management buys this stock enthusiastically with the company's cash and not at all with its own.
6. **Negative tangible equity of −$14.3 billion.** Years of buybacks have consumed the balance sheet. This is a deliberate, rational choice for a business with 71% returns on capital and no need for assets — but it means there is no asset floor under the shares. None.
7. **A downward guidance revision on 2026-08-04**, the first of the window.
8. **The buyback is currently under water.** $7.4 billion deployed in the first half at an average of about $173, against $170.32 today.

**🟢 Green flags**

1. **Elite and *improving* unit economics.** Return on invested capital 71%. Capital spending 1.1% of revenue. Stock compensation 2.1% of revenue — one sixth of Airbnb's 12.9%. Cash earnings run 1.37x accounting earnings. Margins expanded in both years of the window.
2. **A 7-for-7 beat record**, delivered with narrow guidance ranges rather than wide ones.
3. **Management quantifies its own headwinds unprompted** — two percentage points from the war in Q1 2026, currency bridged to the point every quarter.
4. **The transformation programme is over-delivering.** Launched November 2024; $550 million of run-rate savings by the end of 2025 (the high end of guidance); **raised to approximately $650 million on 2026-08-04**, with the extra $100 million landing mostly in 2027.
5. **The lock-in metrics are still improving while growth slows** — a genuinely important divergence. Direct booking mix held stable in the mid-60% range with direct room nights still growing. Genius Level 2 and 3 members are more than 30% of the active base and now account for a *high* 50% share of room nights, up year over year. Merchant-of-record share of gross bookings reached 73%, **up four percentage points year over year**. The customers are getting stickier even as the cohort gets smaller.
6. **Artificial intelligence is already paying on the cost line.** Voice support is scaled across the majority of eligible inbound calls; customer-service cost per booking is falling at a double-digit rate.
7. **The disintermediation fear is measurably not showing up.** Traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid, is "significantly below 1% of our room nights" and "hasn't moved so much recently" (2026-08-04). Booking is inside the new channels, not outside them: a participant in OpenAI's cost-per-click test group and among the first partners in Google's agentic booking rollout.
8. **Unusual disclosure candour on capital allocation** — publishing the multi-year average buyback price of $93 and the half-year average of $173 is not required and is not flattering.

---

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

**The vocabulary moved from "competitive advantage" to "protect."** In Q1 2025, agentic AI was a possible source of cheaper customer acquisition. By Q2 2026, Steenbergen's framing is explicitly defensive: "it's very important to protect customers that are coming direct to us… so that they can have that experience, that full experience in our environment." He catches himself mid-sentence — "actually not protect the direct channel but further expand the direct channel" — which is the most revealing half-second in six calls.

**Fogel now volunteers Google as the precedent, not the threat.** In Q4 2025: "we've been competing, so to speak, with a top-of-the-funnel player who's very big for a very long time… They've made very good money setting up an auction format for taking advertising, and we have been more than happy to pay a lot of money." He then predicts the language-model companies will do the same — "take it high above, don't become a merchant of record." By Q2 2026 he claims that prediction as correct: "I thought that one of them would start going for a performance marketing advertising platform, which is right in our wheelhouse… and they have." This is the bull case and the bear case in one paragraph. If agents become an advertising auction, Booking wins — it is the best bidder in the world. If agents become the merchant of record, Booking loses the customer. Fogel is betting on the first, explicitly and on the record.

**A revealing asymmetry in the second-quarter 2026 AI disclosure.** Third-party data says Booking's brands *appear* frequently in language-model outputs, but "the referrals aren't showing much." Fogel's reading — "we hope it actually reminds people when they do get ready to book" — is a hope, and he labels it as one. Visibility without referral traffic is either latent brand value or a leak. Nobody knows yet, including him.

**Capital allocation is now the loudest signal management sends.** Retiring roughly $14–15 billion a year against a $132 billion market value is an implicit statement that management believes the shares are worth materially more than the tape. They paid $173 on average in the first half. They did not stop when the price fell.

**Continuity of voice.** Fogel (26 years at the company as of February 2026) and Steenbergen have presented every call in the window together. There are no new voices, no departures, no restatements, no auditor changes.

---

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE.**

Not strengthening — every disclosed volume metric has decelerated for five consecutive quarters, and the third-quarter guide of 3–5% room nights is the slowest in the window. Not deteriorating — margins are still expanding, the efficiency programme was raised rather than trimmed, cash conversion is elite and improving, and the stickiness metrics (direct mix, Genius share of room nights, merchant-of-record share) all moved the right way in the same quarter that growth slowed.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing.** You are not underwriting Booking's earnings power; that is visible, high-quality and well disclosed. You are underwriting **one unresolved question: whether artificial-intelligence agents become an advertising auction that Booking wins, or a booking layer that routes around it.** Management has taken a public, specific position on that question and is backing it with roughly $14–15 billion a year of its own buying. The evidence available today supports them — under 1% of room nights come via language models and that share is not moving, while direct mix holds and merchant-of-record share climbs. But the evidence is *early*, and management has declined four times to quantify the one metric that would settle it.

Size to the fact that this question will not be answered inside a quarter. It will be answered over years, by the product decisions of two or three companies that are not Booking.

**Economic moat: WIDE. Moat trend: STABLE.**

The moat type is a **two-sided network with switching costs layered on top**. The network: roughly 31 million accommodation listings, including 8.6 million alternative-accommodation listings, against hundreds of millions of travellers — neither side can be replicated without the other. The switching costs are the newer and more interesting part: Genius members in the top two tiers now account for a high 50% share of room nights and book more often, cancel less and book further ahead; the merchant-of-record share at 73% means Booking holds the payment relationship, the service obligation and the refund liability, which is exactly the messy, regulated, capital-consuming work Fogel argues language models will not want.

**The width judgement rests on the returns evidence, and that evidence points one way.** Return on invested capital is 71% and has not fallen. Operating return on assets is 33.9%. Adjusted margins expanded 193 basis points in 2025 and roughly 40 more basis points in the second quarter of 2026. Capital intensity is 1.1% of revenue, stock compensation 2.1%. This is the opposite of an eroding moat, where you would expect falling returns and margin defended by cuts. Here returns are flat-to-up and the margin is funded by a savings programme management keeps *raising*.

**The trend is stable rather than widening**, and that distinction is deliberate.
